She threw a bundle of money into her stove, because it was cheaper than buying firewood.
You see, this is Germany in 1923, and money is losing its value faster than anyone can spend it.
You see, this is Germany in nineteen twenty-three, and money is losing its value faster than anyone can spend it.
At the end of 1922, a loaf of bread in Berlin cost about 160 marks.
At the end of nineteen twenty-two, a loaf of bread in Berlin cost about one hundred and sixty marks.
By September, the same loaf cost one and a half million, and by November, two hundred billion.
Workers get paid, push their wages home in wheelbarrows, and run straight to the shops before the prices change again.
Kids stack bundles of cash like building blocks, and some families even paper their walls with it.
Her neighbor laughs and goes, why are you burning money?
Her neighbor laughs and goes, why are you burning money?
She just points at the price tag on the firewood.
Fair point.
So where was all this money coming from?
The government owed huge debts, so it did the easiest thing it could think of, and printed more money, day and night.
Think of a pizza.
Cut it into eight slices or eight hundred, and it's still the same pizza, every slice just gets thinner.
That's exactly what happened to every mark in Germany.
Then, in November, they tried something almost funny.
They printed brand new money, crossed out twelve zeros, and one trillion old marks became one new mark.
And it worked, because this time, they promised to do the one thing that actually mattered.
Stop printing.
